Results: plant height and above-ground biomass from UAV LiDAR and VNIR

Built 2026-10-13 18:03 from Biomass_Height_2026-10-09\results and the model folders. Features = feature-based machine learning; Deep learning = two-stream network. All numbers are on held-out test plots.

Summary of all scenarios

How to read the numbers. R², RMSE and rRMSE (RMSE as % of the mean) are computed on all test plots of the 10 cross-validation folds together; every plot is a test plot exactly once and was never seen by the model that predicted it. Height is scored only on the flight with a ruler measurement. Biomass is one overall result pooled over the flights of the scenario. R² depends on how different the pooled flights are: scenario S2 includes AGT maturity, whose mean biomass is much higher, so its R² is larger at about the same rRMSE - compare R² within a scenario and rRMSE across scenarios.

Data preprocessing and quality control

Both modalities are cleaned per plot before any feature is computed. Flagged points and unusable spectral values are kept out of every feature; missing values are never filled in.

LiDAR

Flight-level checks (reported, not altered): coordinate reference system present; points more than 10 m outside the 1st-99th height percentile band; share of single returns (the Ouster cloud is 100 % single-return, so return-based metrics are not used); ground classes, scan angles, flight-line IDs and GPS time encoding; with surveyed GCPs, the vertical consistency of the cloud between GCP pairs.

Per plot (the plot polygon plus a 0.25-1.0 m alley ring, neighbouring plots excluded):

  1. Noise - points more than 30 cm above the plot's 99.9th height percentile are flagged as noise (class 7). They are marked, not deleted, and every metric ignores them.
  2. Ground - a robust plane through the alley ring (5th percentile of height in 25 cm cells), refined with in-plot points within ±8 cm; points with |h| ≤ 8 cm are ground (class 2).
  3. Height normalisation - h = z − plane(x, y).
  4. Canopy - h > 10 cm is canopy (class 5); 8-10 cm is low vegetation (class 3).
  5. Features on canopy points only: height percentiles, canopy-top P90/P95/P99 (5 cm cell maxima, 15 cm edge trim), density layers, cover, voxel volume, gap fraction and LAI proxy −ln(Pgap)/0.5 (also on the 20 cm-trimmed plot interior, because the polygons include alley soil), rumple, roughness, intensity normalised by the alley ground.
Why not statistical outlier removal? On the validation flight (about 30,000 points/m²) every statistical-outlier variant removed sparse canopy tips (heads and awns; 0.3-1.5 % of points, half of them in the top 5 % of the canopy) and lowered the correlation of canopy-top P95 with the ruler height from r 0.70 (unfiltered) to 0.68-0.66. The gap rule flagged a single point in the whole trial.

The LiDAR rules explained

1. Gross-outlier check (whole flight, report only). The 1st (p1) and 99th (p99) elevation percentiles of all points are computed, and points below p1 − 10 m or above p99 + 10 m are counted. Percentiles are used because the minimum and maximum are themselves set by the outliers (one bird return at +80 m makes the maximum useless as a reference). A 10 m margin catches only gross errors: birds, dust or insects in the air, multipath returns below the ground, sensor glitches. Grade: PASS below 0.01 % of the points, WARN below 0.1 %, FAIL otherwise (the flight needs cleaning or checking first).

2. Noise rule ('gap', per plot). The 99.9th elevation percentile (p99.9) of the plot's points is computed, and any point more than 30 cm above it is flagged as noise (class 7). At about 30,000 points/m² a plot holds a few hundred thousand points, so p99.9 is effectively the top of the canopy, with only a few hundred points above it. Real heads and awns form a continuous layer at that level; a point 30 cm above the canopy top with empty air in between cannot be plant material. A neighbour-distance (statistical outlier) filter instead flags wherever points are sparse, which in a cereal canopy is exactly the real tips of heads and awns. Flagged points stay in the file (class 7, withheld flag in the written LAS) so they can be inspected; every height, cover and gap metric skips them.

3. Ground plane (per plot). The ground under a closed canopy is invisible, so it is estimated from the alleys around the plot:

  1. Alley ring - the area between 0.25 m and 1.0 m from the plot edge, minus anything within 0.25 m of any plot (neighbours included): bare alley soil without overhanging canopy.
  2. 25 cm cells, 5th percentile - each 25 × 25 cm cell of the ring is represented by the 5th percentile of its elevations, i.e. the soil surface. Not the minimum (a single low multipath point would pull it down) and not the mean (weeds and stubble would lift it).
  3. Robust plane - z = c0 + c1x + c2y fitted to the cell values by least squares; cells more than 2.5 robust standard deviations (from the median absolute deviation) off the plane are rejected and the plane refitted, up to 4 times, which removes cells with a weed, a clod or a wheel rut. A plane is enough because a plot is only a few metres long.
  4. Refinement - points inside the plot within ±8 cm of the ring plane (soil seen through canopy gaps) are added and the plane refitted; the refined plane is kept only if its RMS misfit is below 6 cm, otherwise the ring-only plane is used.
  5. Fallback - with 200 ring points or fewer, the ground is a flat level at the 1st percentile of the plot's own points.

The sidecar JSON of each classified plot LAS records the ground source (ring, ring + in-plot, fallback), the plane coefficients and the RMS misfit.

4. Height normalisation. h = z − plane(x, y), computed for every point with the plane value at that point's own position, so on a sloping plot each point is measured against the ground beneath it, not one average level. Example: ground plane 245.32 m at a spot, head at 246.17 m there → h = 0.85 m. h is written as the HeightAboveGround attribute of the classified LAS.

5. Classes from height above ground.

h class meaning
|h| ≤ 8 cm 2 ground soil, within the tolerance of the ground fit
8 cm < h ≤ 10 cm 3 low vegetation buffer zone where soil and plant cannot be told apart
h > 10 cm 5 canopy the crop; used by every canopy metric
h < −8 cm 1 unclassified below the ground plane (multipath, ruts)
flagged in step 2 7 noise ignored by all metrics

Why 8 cm: it covers the scatter of real soil around a plane (clods, furrows, sowing rows; fit RMS typically a few cm), the ranging noise of the sensor and small plane-fit errors; a tighter value would push genuine soil into 'vegetation'. Why 10 cm: the 8 cm tolerance plus a 2 cm buffer, so only points clearly above the soil count as crop; the 8-10 cm band holds the ambiguous points and is left out of both soil and canopy. Thresholds of 5-15 cm are typical in crop LiDAR studies.

Consequences to keep in mind.
  • Gap fraction (ground points ÷ all points) slightly overestimates soil: leaves or lodged plants within 8 cm of the soil count as ground. The bias is usually small at anthesis and maturity.
  • Crops shorter than about 10 cm (early growth stages) would be mostly lost from the canopy metrics; the thresholds suit these flights but would need lowering for seedling-stage work.
  • A single plane cannot follow raised beds or strong micro-relief inside a plot; heights would then be biased by the bed height. This is not an issue on these trials.

VNIR

  1. Is the flight usable? A cube fails the reflectance check when its median NDVI is below 0.05, or when it is a float cube without a scale factor and NIR above 2 (still radiance). AGT maturity fails this check and has no VNIR features.
  2. Pixel cleaning - a value of 0 is a negative reflectance clipped to zero by the processing software and is treated as missing, not as zero. Three wavelength ranges are never used: 0-415 nm (sensor edge, weak signal), 755-770 nm (O2-A absorption) and 928-962 nm (water-vapour absorption).
  3. Soil mask per flight - NDVI from 800 and 670 nm, split with Otsu's method; threshold bounded to 0.15-0.50; switched off when a senesced canopy shows no soil/crop contrast.
  4. Per-plot rules - a band or index is NaN for a plot when it is valid on fewer than 50 % of the plot's pixels (otherwise the mean would come only from the brighter surviving pixels and be biased high). When 670 nm is valid on 50 % of the pixels or fewer, every index using a red band (620-690 nm) is NaN (red_ok = 0). Plot QC (vnir_qc_ok): more than 90 % of the plot inside the cube, vegetation cover above 0.2, reflectance cube.

Valid and invalid bands

Band validity is decided at three levels, each building on the previous one:

level rule result
Band in a plot outside the three excluded ranges and valid on ≥ 50 % of the plot's pixels per-plot spectra tables (NaN otherwise)
Band for the dataset (common bands) usable on ≥ 95 % of the plots of every reflectance flight 111 bands: 522-645, 691-754, 772-926, 965-1000 nm (networks, spectral PCA families)
Band for the Muresk-only runs the same 95 % rule on the two Muresk flights 138 bands: 469-754, 772-926, 965-1000 nm (142 with the four O2-A bands)
Plot (valid-band scenarios) rule A: all 111 bands valid on ≥ 50 % of pixels + plot QC + reflectance; rule B: ≥ 95 % of pixels and ≥ 95 % of the plot inside the cube rule A 497 plot-flights (S4); rule B 209, Muresk only (S5)

The common list lacks 415-522 nm (blue) and 645-691 nm (red) compared with the Muresk list because those bands are clipped to zero on many AGT anthesis plots - a property of the data, not a design choice.

Comparison with the literature

step status note
Noise → ground → height normalisation → canopy threshold → plot percentile metrics standard usual sequence in crop LiDAR (e.g. Madec et al. 2017; ten Harkel et al. 2020)
Canopy threshold 10 cm standard 5-15 cm is typical
Gap fraction and Beer-Lambert LAI proxy (G = 0.5) standard e.g. Jimenez-Berni et al. 2018 (wheat)
Removing sensor-edge, O2-A and water-vapour bands standard the usual hyperspectral bad-band list
NDVI soil mask with Otsu threshold standard Otsu 1979
log reflectance + SNV before spectral PCA standard common spectroscopy preprocessing (SNV: Barnes et al. 1989)
Ground from a plot-local alley plane adapted most studies use a global ground filter (CSF, PMF, SMRF) or a bare-soil scan; a local plane suits flat trial plots
Gap noise rule instead of statistical outlier removal adapted SOR is the usual choice; replaced after our own test (box above)
Interior gap metrics adapted from our diagnosis that the polygons include alley soil
50 % per-plot and 95 % per-dataset band thresholds own choice reasonable conventions; rarely specified in papers, which often average all pixels or drop bands by inspection
Clipped zeros treated as missing; red-based indices censored own choice sound but rarely discussed
Savitzky-Golay smoothing; BRDF/illumination correction between flights not applied common in the literature; red-edge derivatives here use the raw mean spectrum

Methods in brief

Feature-based models

Per plot, LiDAR v3.2 features (canopy-only height percentiles, canopy-top heights, cover, gap fraction on the plot interior, voxel volume, profile area, rumple, roughness, normalised intensity; about 75-85 columns) and VNIR v3.0.1 features (vegetation-masked spectral indices, reflectance in broad bands, red-edge shape, spectral PCA scores; about 130 columns; unusable bands and the indices built on them are NaN and leave the model), plus the mean vegetation spectrum (log reflectance, standardised per plot) over the bands valid on at least 95 % of the plots. These are grouped into feature families per category:

  • LiDAR only: LiDAR core (22-32 selected features, random-forest selection of the top 10-12 inside each training fold), LiDAR all (height only), and LiDAR PCA.
  • VNIR only: VNIR core (selected indices), VNIR PCA (all VNIR features) and VNIR bands PCA (the spectrum itself).
  • Fused: fused core, fused all (selection), Fused PCA (one PCA per modality, components joined), Fused PCA joint (one PCA on LiDAR + VNIR together) and Fused bands PCA (LiDAR PCA + spectrum PCA).

PCA. In every family marked PCA, each block of features is standardised and reduced to the principal components that keep 95 % of its variance; the scaler and the PCA are fitted inside each training fold only, so a test plot never influences them, and the learner sees only the components. Typically about 80 LiDAR features become 10-12 components, about 130 VNIR features 9-18, and the spectrum 2-7. The tables 'Models chosen' below show, per scenario, how often a PCA family was among the chosen models.

Learners per family: ridge, PLS, Gaussian process, random forest, extra trees, LightGBM. Top three per category, nested: inside each outer training fold a 5-fold inner loop scores every family x learner of the category, and the three best are fitted on the outer training plots and averaged on the outer test plots. Biomass feature models are fitted per flight; their test predictions are pooled for the overall result.

Deep learning

Two-stream network: a sparse 3D convolutional network on the classified plot point cloud (2 cm voxels; height above ground, normalised intensity, return number) and a transformer on 512 vegetation pixel spectra per plot (fixed common band list, log reflectance standardised per pixel, band-availability mask), joined with a trial/stage embedding into a regression head. Variants: LiDAR only, VNIR only, two-stream (fused). 100 epochs per fold, AdamW, one-cycle learning rate, training-time augmentation (rotation, mirroring, point dropout, jitter, pixel bootstrap, brightness). One network is trained on all flights of a scenario together.

Validation

10-fold cross-validation, folds grouped by plot (both flights of a plot always fall in the same fold) and stratified by flight. The overall result uses all test plots; the fold tables show each fold's own test set. Fold-wise R² is shown for completeness: with 13 test plots per fold (height, Muresk) it is unstable, so read the fold RMSE.

S1. Plant height - Muresk maturity flight

Data

128 wheat plots of the Muresk NUE trial flown on 2025-11-21 (maturity). Inputs per plot: LiDAR v3.2 features of the classified plot cloud, VNIR v3.0.1 features and the mean vegetation spectrum (bands valid on at least 95 % of the plots).
